Sports.title: Sir Billy Boston obituary
Sports.summary: First rugby league player to be knighted who was an explosive winger for Wigan and Great Britain Sir Billy Boston, who has died aged 92, was one of the greatest, and most popular, rugby league players of all time. A rambunctious, explosive powerhouse of a winger for Great Britain and Wigan during the 1950s and 60s, he would leave trails of bedraggled tacklers in his wake with his blockbusting runs, while his robust defensive work often left opponents dazed. With Boston’s strength, though, came great pace and handling skills, allied to a swerve and sidestep that few were able to counter. As a result he was a prodigious scorer of tries – 571 in 562 matches across a 17-year career in which he won a World Cup with Great Britain as well as three Challenge Cups and a league championship with Wigan. Culture.title: Jill Gomez obituary
Culture.summary: Soprano with razor-sharp articulation who created lead roles including the Duchess of Argyll in Powder Her Face A lustrous vocal quality, combined with an alluring, exuberant stage presence, ensured the popularity of the soprano Jill Gomez, who has died aged 83, on both operatic stage and concert platform. When her talent came to the fore in the early 1970s she was hailed by Arthur Jacobs in Opera magazine, along with Josephine Barstow, as “the most exciting of our newer female singers”, while reviews of the time hailed her Governess in Britten’s The Turn of the Screw and Anne Trulove in Stravinsky’s The Rake’s Progress as among the finest. The latter role was one of those she took, along with Mélisande, Calisto and Helena (A Midsummer Night’s Dream), at Glyndebourne, where Gomez enjoyed her first major successes, appearing between 1969 and 1984. At Covent Garden her roles included Lisa in La Sonnambula, Titania in A Midsummer Night’s Dream and Lauretta in Puccini’s Gianni Schicchi. Continue reading...

Culture.title: ‘The whole world is becoming rightwing and anti-gay’: William Yang on 60 years of capturing LGBTQ+ life
Culture.summary: Yang has taken more than 500,000 photographs since he first moved to Sydney in the late 1960s and now devotes most of his time to untangling the past As a young adult, William Yang discovered that his family’s story was actually a murder mystery. His uncle, William Fang Yuen, was killed by an employee on the family’s farm in far north Queensland in 1922, but his mother refused to tell him the full story. In 1990, he travelled to Innisfail in search of the truth. One aunt told Yang that his uncle and the worker had got into a fight over a gambling debt, and the worker had stabbed him to death with a spear. A cousin said a gang was involved. A local woman, who had been a child at the time, remembered it as a card game gone wrong. Continue reading...
